Zenith Standard Time (ZST) would be a boon for health, sociability, safety, and business. With today's technology it would be trivial to automatically coordinate cross-country communications and travel. 

As article states;

Before U.S. railroads introduced standard time zones in 1883, towns set their clocks to strike noon when the sun reached its zenith overhead. As The New York Times put it that November, if clocks had rung an alarm at local noon from Maine to the Pacific, “there would have been a continuous ringing from the east to the west lasting for 3¼ hours.”

Just think: a cross-country trip could take literally no time!

I have a PhD in Food Science and I'm board-certified in preventive medicine. All of a sudden "ultra-processed" is the bogeyman when the problem is salt, sugar and saturated fat, just as it has been for decades. 

If the FDA really wanted to inform the public about the risks in the food they eat, they would set maximum levels of salt, sugar and saturated fat per serving. As an example, if a can of baked beans had more than 300 mg of sodium per serving, that would require a warning label like those on cigarette packages.

Simply labeling something as "ultraprocessed" is meaningless. A piece of cheese is ultraprocessed because most people cannot make it in their home kitchen. Similarly, hamburger is ultraprocessed because most people cannot make it in their home kitchen. 

We need to stop the nonsense and focus upon the problem components: salt, sugar and saturated fats.

In the absence of good leadership, the bulk of the work towards coexistence and reconciliation comes from pragmatic efforts within the civil society sector. Organizations like CISEPO (www.cisepo.ca), which works across borders to improve quality of life through access to good health care, and the other ones mentioned in this article (i.e., ecopeace, etc.) work tirelessly with little funding and under incomprehensible conditions to address this. However, there's an ideological movement gaining traction that pits itself against efforts to improve the practicalities of life, such as health system resilience and reach. The claim is that it conditions those benefiting to accept structural violence or inequity. It does not. Teaching it and advocating for it regenerates a black hole. In actuality, conditioning people to accept a poor quality of life and reduced basic conditions just perpetuates suffering and, downstream, the inability to effect change, while leaving those who are most vulnerable to suffer and lose agency. Yes, we do need the governance roundtables, the dignitaries, and the splash of star power, and we do need the structural changes of a legitimized peace process to reinforce improved conditions. A good mayor of a major U.S. city could generate political will around that. But efforts that are proximate to the need and engage civil society are where the power to change lies.

The first encounter with his men is where the fear in her eyes is real: she pleads to not hurt her and her eyes, her entire being is telling us how women have been treated then...she is beautiful, it is a different kind of beauty and different kind of seduction, a more complex and real than sex - flattery and praise of men and their bravery and strength...and all of them succumb and Odysseus is close...yet she sees in him something else...it is a complex dance of wills and powers, fear and seduction, threats and defenses... Again, one can come to a theater with a notion and let that notion drive the experience, or one can come open to a new experience...one may not enjoy it, it may not be their cup of tea, and it is ok. comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
I am compelled to respond when people argue countries do not manage forests & unprecedented fires better. It is bad information & misleading. It relies on finding simple villains.

In n. hemisphere large parts of Europe are drying out, desertification is creeping from Africa to the northern mediterranean.

Canada's vast sparsely populated boreal forests, over a million contiguous square miles from Nova Scotia to British Columbia/Yukon, are drying out.

The same goes for Russia's  larger boreal forests.

Southerly areas of permfrost are melting. The arctic is heating 3+ times faster than elsewhere. Agricultural growing zones are moving north.

All global trends are moving in a clear and persistent direction.

We are privileged to live within a range of ecological conditions and environmental constraints. These are being exceeded due to climate change. Our infrastructure was designed to function within min - max constraints, exceed criteria and it doesn’t function adaquately.

Many people essentially say there is nothing new under the sun (Ecleissiates). The thing is the tide goes in & out and "it gets hot, it gets cold" not by chance but established proven principles.

Popular bias and convention are problems for science. I get it, we don't like massive unprecedented change, we want stasis, but denying climate change with simple convienent views is blind and anti science. Views that will lead society to the dust heap of history as historians & geologist say.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Many people are simply unaware of the scale of the threat which climate change poses to humanity.

The carbon cycle for the last 2 million years was doing 180-280ppm atmospheric CO2 over 10,000 years and we’ve done more change than that in 100 years.

The last time CO2 went from 180-280ppm global temperature increased by around 4 degrees C and sea level rose 130 meters. (graph of the last 400,000 years of global temperature, CO2 and sea level https://www.ces.fau.edu/nasa/images/impacts/slr-co2-temp-400000yrs.jpg )

One amplifying feedback alone out of dozens, loss of albedo or heat reflectivity from Arctic summer sea ice melt, over the last several decades has been equivalent to 25 percent of the climate forcing of anthropogenic CO2. And that will continue to increase as that ice largely disappears by mid century.

The Titanic sank because by the time the lookout called the warning the ship had too much momentum to turn. The Earth has a lot more momentum, e.g. we've already likely locked in at least 6 meters of sea level rise from the marine sectors of Greenland and West Antarctica’s ice sheets, and decade to decade warming in the near term is also virtually locked in.

That momentum is building and the higher we let global temperatures rise the greater the risk of them going really high as amplifying feedbacks strengthen.

I’m a part of nature too and I wonder why a healthy and vibrant flower cared for by a loving gardener isn’t vain but I am? I know a flower didn’t put effort into it in the same way but still.
I don’t think the beauty industry preying on everyone is a good thing and I don’t think we should go into debt for it or experience despair at the sign of every wrinkle but why not try to put love and care into my skin too? Thoughtfully and lovingly. Most of what I do actively makes my skin healthier.
I still have no idea how to navigate it all but I really appreciate this article and it made me feel less alone in the slightly unusual (or maybe just not talked about) motivations behind that bottle of vitamin C on my counter.

But I'm not touching my face right now. Not yet, at least. I've seen the beauty in growing old gracefully - I saw it on my father before he died. And I saw how youth can be taken in an instant. The utter, overwhelming tragedy of that. All life is fleeting. But precious. Aging is a part of this journey we're on, and I wish more women would just embrace their age. Welcome it even! And maybe when we look in the mirror, we don't see all that we've lost. But all that we are still *becoming*. That is truly the greatest gift of all.

If I had put the gazillions (exagerating, but not by much), I spent from the age of 13 to 60, on serums, makeup, potions and lotions, dermatologists(!), and other promisers of fantastic "maintenence", etc.,etc., and instead put it in an interest bearing account, I'd be thinking about island beach real estate now.

The point, the soul, of this piece is not really about preserving youth and beauty. It is about the futile quest to stave of the inevitable and to remain visible while trying to do so. The author's mother is a totem in this journey, as are all of our parents. 

I hated my bulging knuckles for decades, then I realized they were exactly like my father's. Now I look at them in bittersweet happiness as a daily reminder of him whenever I use my hands.

Later on, when I experimented myself, not only did it feel like a waste of time, but I also found out that I'm allergic to most products that you put on your face. I also just hated how fake I felt.

From then on, I never wear makeup. I'm just me, no makeup, 100% of the time. I guess I'm looksmaxxing natural beauty. I'm not a showstopper by any means, but I don't get hung up on whether my appearance is important all the time. It doesn't matter.

My mother died last year at 97. She had a long and love filled life. She lived all of the suggestions laid out in this article. Life past 92 for her, unfortunately, was painful to watch. Falls and hospital stays became the norm. 

Which made me think about smart aging. How smart?  Why does this society put off thinking about death to the point of blind denial of the obvious.  My wonderful mother was in full denial that she would someday pass on, right to the end. We fill our hearts with potential immortality. If we just eat right, exercise and are lucky enough to not suffer Alzheimer’s or other mind erasing diseases, we could live on forever. Life after 90, for most people lucky enough to make 90, is painful and difficult to watch, let alone live. 

Everyone’s journey is different but let’s not send people into old age with the belief that if I follow healthy tenets I can live as long as I want without suffering.  Dying in my sleep at 90 sounds pretty good to me.

In December, my wife and I invested in an industrial quality treadmill with a screen. I've been using it consistently at least 5x/week since March, and I also created a custom LLM "coach" in NotebookLM that analyzes my Garmin sleep and exercise data, and the diet data I enter in Cronometer. 

One of the things that has helped me maintain this consistently is the screen. I get on the treadmill and stream my favorite TV. Plot-driven shows are especially good, because they drive you forward, make you want to stay on the treadmill. 

This has changed my life. I've lost about ten pounds, and I feel much stronger and I'm sleeping better. I've lost most of the gut. In fact I feel the best I've felt in decades. I get up in the morning feeling like I'm 30 again. 

I can't believe I waited this long to get into an exercise regimen.

As a winemaker in northern California, climate change and fires have become somewhat of a regularity for our industry. I cannot recall a vintage in almost the last decade that hasn't experienced some fire-related pressure. Our mantra has become "make the wine when you can", and when the vintage and yields are good, we do. 

These fires are coming amidst a very strong El Niño event; layer on top of it the continuing effects of climate change and the ingredients for fire conditions are prime.

Sadly this is normal for our industry now. Yet, our greatest existential challenge is finding a niche with the modern consumer. As most would-be wine drinkers change their relationship with alcohol, the wine industry is caught in yet another cycle of pivoting and adaptation. For many it is a gloomy time as wineries sell off, but I like to remind that wine has been adapting for centuries. From rock sheltered plantings in the Canary Islands, to the phylloxera crises, to wars and everything between, we are farmers and we find a way.

That can only happen in a competitive but regulated environment. 

The failures have been characterised by capitalism metamorphosing into an obsession with the economies of scale opening the way to the death of competition and the domination of every sector by uncompetitive oligopolies that maintain high prices and appalling customer service. 

Socialism has been characterised by an overweening role for government leading to over regulation, the stifling of energy, innovation and enterprise.

Companies that have failed to meet the terms of their licenses to operate should be denied that right. Firms like Thames Water should long ago have been stripped of the licenses, denied the right to operate and their franchises offered to companies that were not solely self serving.

There needs to be a new accountability in business that channels but does not kill the animal spirits that spur entrepreneurship.

Incubation periods, the nature of the agent, and the ability of physicians to diagnose swiftly all determine whether lives can be saved.

The statement cited near the end of the article that: “Chinese companies are not doing open source for the sake of open source itself; they are employing it at as a strategy, as a tool of the challenger”, is applicable to companies in all nations but it expresses only a half truth.  

In reality, open source programming has been more like a university spread around the world, offering free education to all.

This is behind the development of prominent open source software in many areas such as  word processing and multimedia players, including one in the new category AI, namely DeepSeek.  Wikipedia is of a similar type origin, an early competitor to expensive encyclopedia.  

Open source today is now of key value in the development of poor nations

The team of volunteer people, and now many paid people, around the world who check and help regulate open sources products, deserve thanks for their contributions. 

China, like India, the U.S., Japan, and South Korea, is special because its contributions to open source can accelerate the benefits, and heartaches, of AI to all nations, including itself.

The genius of Bill Gates was not as a coder or engineer.

Instead, Gates made the MSDOS source code freely available so that any programmer in the world could build games and applications that could only run on MS DOS (i.e., not Apple DOS).

Thus, when Microsoft teamed up with IBM to bundle MS DOS with the IBM PC (and every PC clone thereafter), they beat out Apple in the apps market, and generated enormous revenue streams -- which live on today with Windows.

This is an analogy of what China's Moonshot is doing.

Chinese open weight models are helping narrow one of the biggest AI divides: the gap between organizations that can afford frontier models and those that cannot. That is a positive development for innovation and competition.

At the same time, we should broaden the discussion beyond the usual concerns of privacy and security. A more subtle risk is cognitive influence. What if a model consistently nudges users toward polarization, individualism, or other value systems? The issue is not only what an AI knows, but the assumptions it quietly reinforces at scale.

For this reason, I found Pope Leo’s latest book particularly thought-provoking. Whether or not you share its perspective, it raises questions every technology leader should be asking. Highly recommended as a weekend read.

Kimi K3 is undeniably good tech held hostage by a government that can't decide if it wants Chinese AI to conquer the world or stay locked in a compound. "Open" is doing a lot of lying here: you can see the code, you just can't run it without a license and a chip allocation Beijing might yank anyway. That's not open source, that's a demo with a paywall and a leash.

Ask Kimi about June 4, 1989 and you'll get a wall, a redirect, or historical amnesia dressed up as a "sensitive topic." Ask about Taiwan and it'll recite the CCP's one-China script like it's reading from a Party memo, because it is. That's the tell: a model that can write code as well as GPT but can't tell you who runs Taiwan's government without genuflecting to Zhongnanhai isn't a technological triumph, it's state media with better math skills.

Can they out-compete Silicon Valley? On benchmarks, increasingly yes. On trust, no chance, because any system built to lie by design about its own government's atrocities will lie about whatever else serves the Party next. That's not a bug you patch, it's the whole architecture.

"People who are not professional historians sometimes assume that historical research is a once-and-for-all process that will eventually produce a single, final version of what happened in the past. We often hear charges of “revisionism” when a familiar history seems to be challenged or changed. But revisiting and often revising earlier interpretations is actually at the very core of what historians do. And that’s because the present is continually changing." 
https://ncph.org/what-is-public-history/how-historians-work/the-changing-past/
[National Council on Public History]

History is chaotic and particularly for the span of our lifetimes.

We are too close to readily understand the events.   Where in a Nation one is may expose different local standards for textbooks or even different attitudes in differing communities within a State or a Canadian Province.   How Alberta sees the Canadian Dominion likely is quite different from that way Quebec sees matters.    I expect that events in Paris or in Arles or in Champagne see different takes within France.

History is a mish-mosh of holdings and the Black community has its various takes even amongst its generation.

Colson Whitehead can only add to the conversation, but his voice, while important, may not fully establish a new standard, even as it creates an important focus of attention and the substantial contribution to the general discussion that should always be at hand!

These small and medium sized business are crushed by health insurance costs and employee retention challenges directly linked to the Trump administration’s evisceration of our social safety net. Here in Vermont small businesses and school districts have difficulty attracting employees because hedge funds buy a large percentage of houses that come on the market and then rent them out at exorbitant rates. “Affordability” must be presented as support for small and medium sized businesses. Democrats could then identify themselves as the party that is pro-business and makes the real economy run. I would expect markets to reverse course when hedge fund managers and institutional traders subsequently step in to readjust their positions. At least, that’s how I would read it.

Whether new technologies prove to be a giant bubble or a new industrial revolution, at a minimum, I suspect fierce competition will likely cause several overfunded AI companies and their supply chains to fail, resulting in financial turmoil. Perhaps governments should consider imposing excise taxes on these firms' revenues and on the capital they raise during an IPO to create contingency reserves that would help absorb potential financial shocks and mitigate any social and environmental harms.

I live here.  Kumamoto Castle was already damaged in the devastating double-quake ten years ago, and now, just months after the 10 year celebration of the city's recovery, another almost identical disaster has happened.  Thousands of people are without access to water or power, in a summer where the afternoons are regularly hitting 95-98 degrees F, with humidity so intense you could choke, so suffocating that even sweat doesn't help you cool down.  A mall barely half an hour from my house collapsed, and then exploded in the aftermath, trapping dozens inside.  There was a preschool on the second floor of that mall.  We think the children made it out, but we don't know.  And the whole region is waiting with baited breath, because the last time this happened, in 2016, the first earthquake wasn't the worst.  Even when the aftershocks had calmed, the worst damage came a day later, with a second quake even stronger than the first.

We watched our city's symbol of resilience crumble today.  But the lessons Kumamoto and the greater island of Kyushu learned 10 years ago also mean that we have opened shelters and emergency provisioning stations faster than the last time.  My community responded within minutes that everyone was accounted for and uninjured.  We are shaken, but still standing.

And hoping desperately that the next week will be on stable ground.

comments.body: Wow, so surprising and heartening to learn that Frank Serpico is still alive and is finally being given public recognition for his valorous efforts over fifty years ago to expose corruption within the NYC police force. It sounds like he was forced jnto hiding for many years to avoid retribution for his efforts, and is still keeping a very low profile. There may be as many corrupt cops as there ever were, in NYC and elsewhere, but at the very least, we, the residents of these cities, are more aware of the issue in our encounters with sketchy officers of the law.  Forewarned is forearmed. I humbly thank you, Mr. Serpico, for having the courage to tear the blinds from our eyes.

comments.name: mb
comments.body: There is a new sheriff in town…

comments.name: Marine1975
comments.body:
The acknowledgement by Sheriff Raymond, of Detective Frank Serpico, touched me.

As a native NYC, Italian-American kid, not long returned from Vietnam, “Serpico” made an impression.  

Frank’s story  gave idealistic men and women a share in the sacrifice and upheavals - heavy costs - of doing the right thing; speaking up, when malfeasance, abuse or simple incompetence were ignored, or blatantly supported by ambivalent superiors.

Sixty years later, many of us still “suffer” that addiction…that inability to ignore the unjustifiable abuse or neglect of prima facia evidence of intolerance or wrongdoing.

Very grateful that Sheriff Raymond made Frank Serpico his “North star,” and that Mayor Mamdani  was present to acknowledge Frank’s good conscience and significant sacrifice.

comments.name: H. Emma

Thank you for this lovely, heartening article! It actually brought me to tears - absurd, but people like these two gentlemen are all too rare, and Frank Serpico, especially, has suffered for it. 

I wish our new sheriff well!

Is there any upside to this climate change disaster?

Cutting down on flammable vegetation would help.  Notwithstanding DJT’s advice, raking probably is not enough.

However, goats would help, though Europe will need them to breed like, um, randy goats.

The other bright spot:  The Gulf Stream is weakening.  If so, Europe will have the climate of Greenland - though Spain and Italy may be closer to Newfoundland.

Which will be chilly for awhile.  But in a generation or two, it may be just right.

Hope that cheers Europe up.

comments.name: Martha
comments.body: At the local level, individuals who rise to the occasion to help their neighbors are heroic, but this problem is global and it's interconnected with the dominant power structure. I believe these wildfires that are engulfing countries on an intercontinental scale, along with the melting glaciers and drying up of the planet, should be alerting us to the reality that we are entering a new age of ecological collapse brought on by accelerated resource extraction and consumption and destruction of natural, sustaining systems. That in combination with growing feedback loops, and governments' unwillingness and apparent inability to respond appropriately, point to the fact that we are really not prepared for what we are up against.

comments.name: Canis candida
comments.body: It should be regularly recognized, what Bernie Sanders has been saying for a long time now, that Democratic Socialists are asking for things that most Americans want. Taxing the rich is a very very obvious and reasonable thing to ask for. The current situation, in which fabulously wealthy people get away with paying little in taxes, not only looks unfair, it looks nonsensical. So it's quite possible that the DSA will be successful in getting a majority of voters on their side. And not just in New York State.

comments.name: Lulu
comments.body: Why do “Democratic Socialists” get to run in Democratic primaries? They have their own party, they should run their own primaries.

comments.name: Oxfdblue
comments.body:
I support many of the DSA's objectives despite not identifying myself as a Socialist.  Somewhat higher taxes on very wealthy New Yorkers (income over $2 million), sure.  

More renewable energy sources- absolutely.  State takeover of Con Ed...not going to happen. Con Ed is a publicly traded company and has a market cap of over $41 billion.  How does such a state takeover work?  Who pays the stockholders who are not all multimillionaires.

No non-profit status for any organization with even the slightest tie to Israel. No. Forget it.  Would that include synagogues?  If so, then what about the tax exempt status for other religious organizations.  Also, such a ban would easily be struck down in court as a violation of free speech.  

Right now, the current Israeli government is truly horrible.  They are guilty of war crimes at the very least, and a good case for genocide certainly exists.  But what some DSA members are asking for comes across as not action against the Israeli government, but action against every Jewish organization out there...and therefore it's not anti-Israel, but anti-Jewish. 

The DSA has some really good ideas but like all parties that push the political envelope, they need to learn compromise and abolish their insane purity tests.  They will politically kill a candidate/official who only (!) agrees with 99.9% of their agenda.

comments.name: common sense advocate
comments.body:
This democrat and dozens of others I know are disgusted with the mayor's focus on party politics and diatribes about Israel, while homelessness languishes at before seen levels on his watch.

He shut down two major homeless resources before finding alternatives for highly vulnerable people. And he has deliberately slowed moving people out of street encampments and into supportive services with seven day delays. There's one encampment on broadway and 75th street that's been there for months. There's nothing socialist about people sick and dirty and begging on the street, it's just inhumane.

And now the trash is overflowing because his empire bin strategy with key card locks that don't let passersby dump trash - added to corner trash can reductions - give pedestrians fewer places to put garbage. 

That's poor focus on the city he was elected to run and poor organization of our resources. 

You earn the privilege of pitching socialist party dogma when you have achievements on behalf of the people you are elected to serve.

We know he had no experience running a business or a budget, but he really needs to learn quickly - on behalf of the people of this city. Our poorest and most vulnerable need him to catch up quickly.

comments.name: A

comments.name: Sparky
comments.body:
It's hard for me to understand the DSA's obsession with Israel as anything other than antisemitic.

Housing affordability, health care and income inequality are all vital issues to millions of New Yorkers, but Israel is not. Yet it gets equal time.

Moreover, where is the outrage (or even a peep) about the brutal genocide in Sudan that has slaughtered infinitely more people, the fierce oppression of hundreds of millions of women and gays who live under Middle Eastern dictatorships, the concentration camps in China which torture and murder the Uyghurs to name just a few?

If you listen to the DSA there is only one global issue that matters and it just happens to be how Israel is singularly evil. That type of bias and prejudice is nothing if not antisemitic.

comments.body:
Calling Guyana oil rich makes it sound like Saudi Arabia. It is not. The biggest beneficiary of the oil money is Exon, as they are well known to extract money from poor countries for themselves. The next beneficiary are those in power, who hail to Exon, and their friends who get lucrative contracts. The losers are the poor people in Guyana, which is most of the population. Those who can, leave. Sad.

comments.name: Felicia Persaud
comments.body:
Kudos to the New York Times for its focus on this disaster but a few points. 
1: This is the worst maritime disaster in the Caribbean since 1970.
2: The MV Barima pre-dates Guyana’s independence by 27 years and yet was still in service.
3: The Ma Lisha was commissioned by the president, Irfaan Ally, in 2023 to replace the Barima but was not brought into service on this route.
4: Where are the billions that were approved for the ferry and hinterland infrastructure.
5: Why were no coast guards on scene immediately?
6: Why is the government running ferries with no insurance?
7: Where are the country’s own emergency response services?
8: Why is the government more concerned with increasing the retirement benefits of former presidents?
9: Where are the trauma counselors and assistance to the survivors?
10: Why was no one consulted on this farce of a Commission of Inquiry and why are these ministers not hired or at the very least sent on leave pending the COI! The Guyana regime is a disgrace and should be sued by all survivors!

comments.name: Mrs. G
comments.body: I visited Guyana, the land of my birth, in May. The opportunity there is palpable. However, even with oil money, the country will ultimately implode if the government does not find a way to create true opportunity for the disenfranchised. There is enough to go around. We can do better! My condolences to all impacted by this tragedy.

Thank you for your reporting.

“After I left the prayer service, other Guyanese I had interviewed began sending me reports that Ms. Nageer and other protesters had been arrested by the police and were being charged with unlawful assembly.”

This is hearsay reporting and adds fuel to an already tense situation. I’m wondering if it’s incumbent on reporters to verify such findings before reporting on it. 

“The authorities also arrested Sherod Duncan, an opposition member of Parliament, after he traveled to the site of the disaster and launched a drone to capture aerial footage of recovery vessels and the gathering of families at the waterfront.”

Mr. Duncan was flying his drone and invading the rescue operation space including flying too close to a rescue helicopter. He was arrested and charged with interfering with the rescue operation. 

Furthermore, the opposition knew the ferry was old.  Why didn’t  they speak up and approach the government or the people.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body: A sign of the times, right? A place where anyone (for a modest fee) could go and view art and be nourished by it is now a place for some people to view art as investment and be enriched financially by it. A place whose design was to keep out light to protect the art now looks like a place designed to keep out people to protect buyers and their deals. The museum restaurants were never cheap, museum restaurants never are, but they were part of something fantastic and, at their core, egalitarian, insofar as they were for the museum goers. Times change, don't they. I doubt the patrons of Marcel will be scared away now. Just as I doubt most readers would have gone there before being scared off. So maybe this review is a little useless. It is, however, a good encapsulation of what has happened in our city in general. Money has moved in big time. And an awful lot of tailored suits don't seem to notice that it's not really an improvement.

comments.name: Chantal
comments.body: For the first time in a long time, we know exactly where you stand on this one. You don't like it, you were disappointed, the food is not great, you say so clearly. It's refreshing. Much more useful than a review one has to parse to find a clear statement of evaluation. Which too often happens. The pictures as always make everything look divine. I find that disconcerting. But these days when so much restaurant fare is designed for the eye (well, the camera) and not the palate, the disjunction is inevitable when the food is bad. More surprising are your generalized digs at wealth. I'm neither wealthy nor a fan of wealth, but so many of the places you laud are hugely expensive and cater to wealth. Is it different here? Is it the Sotheby's connection? Are there no irreproachably tailored, oblivious men on computers eating lunch elsewhere? The digs seem mean. Nonetheless, Marcel is only satisfactory. We've been warned. It's not easy to come down hard on a place in an economy in which "satisfactory" could be damaging. I would say though that the reviews as a whole will seem more accurate, more thorough if "satisfactory" isn't only handed out to well-bankrolled places as it has been so far in the new regime, and if the main critics, not just the critics of the mini reviews, aren't shy to use it. Of course, that may require going to a wider range of places, to places that aren't known in advance to be good. For today, though, the evaluation is appreciated. Criticism is useful.

I enjoy rain. I love thunderstorms. I embrace the rainbows that link sun and rain. Thank you for this article. 

Where I grew up, most summer days were capped by a late afternoon thunderstorm that cleared the air.  Here, in coastal Southern California, the mystery is the marine layer — will it move onshore, hide the horizon, or dissipate for the day?  How long after sunrise will the sun come out?

May Gray, June Gloom, No Sky July, and Fog-ust are simply the ocean in the air.  Water picked up by the temperature differential, colder water into warmer breezes.  

A July day without marine layer is going to be really hot, even near the coast.  WITH the marine layer, balmy, possibly chilly.

I’m now thinking about buying a barometer just to see what it says.

We’ve been seeing numerous impacts catching many scientists by surprise with how soon they are occurring. In 2014 two independent teams of scientists reported that the West Antarctic Ice Sheet is likely irreversibly retreating. 10 feet of sea level rise equivalent of ice there is being destabilized by a warming ocean.

The paleoclimate record indicates that increasing global temperature by just 1.5-2 °C above preindustrial temperature commits the system to an eventual 20-30 feet of sea level rise, a large fraction of which could arrive within the next 100 years.

Corals may not survive this century of warming and acidifying oceans, and droughts and floods linked to global warming—and conflict linked to those droughts—have already caused 18 countries to face famine.

Because of the decades to millennial long lag between a climate forcing and our feeling the full effect, due to the thermal inertia of the ocean and response time of the ice sheets, the effects we are feeling now are largely just the beginning of the result of emissions from the 20th century. And emissions have been increasing steadily for decades.

We are also seeing numerous amplifying feedbacks: loss of albedo (heat reflectivity) from ice melt, permafrost melt, methane release and massive wildfires; the Earth is starting to wrest any possible further human control of the climate away.

We're about out of time on this, if not already, and leaders are still acting as if this is not a planetary emergency.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.
